title: my cafe dream, loss, grief, and gifts
content:
a very long, painfully detailed saga (10,837 words) of a coffee shop dream and betrayal I experienced in the fall of 2024 — and how it transformed me.

TABLE OF CONTENTS


introduction

PART I — DREAM LOSS RAGE GRIEF

a coffee shop love story
making the dream happen
all the red flags we ignored
the storm: betrayal and speechless rage
a midnight confrontation with 3 turkish men
the cafe opens, but I feel only grief
then came the bitter end
the death blow was a $10 logo


PART II — THE GIFTS MY BODY LEARNED

on betrayal and self-betrayal
the sacredness of boundaries
on vision, clarity, and alignment
recognition is permission and power
the reversal of creative business flow
after notes: a death and initiation

*

back to top

introduction

today I’m going to tell you (and my future self) the story of how a long time dream to open a coffee shop with my life partner K suddenly materialized, as if out of thin air, like a wish come true — then slowly devolved into a nightmare, evaporating as quickly as it came — but not without creating a vacuum-vortex of disappointment, loss, and rage that woke me up for weeks in full body hives, and consumed the last months of my year.

in this experience, my partner K and I lost, between the two of us: two decades long “brotherly” friendships, months of sanity and creative energy, a feeling of trust, dignity, and respect, and around eight thousand dollars of my money invested and then spent haphazardly by men who called me “their sister.”

it was an emotional and financial trauma, but more than that — it was an energetic violation and betrayal.

the experience felt like a severance of my worth as a creative being — from the money I made from that creative energy. it represented a demolishing of what I’ve so worked hard to integrate for the last decade as an artist-entrepreneur — not the money itself — because money is only the byproduct of my energy — but my sense of worth in a capitalist world; the integrity, vision, and creative life source which made me that money in the first place.

perhaps what enraged me the most — was that it felt like a misogynistic refutation of my worth as a sovereign being with agency over her own resources. it was two egotistical men saying to me — your money is NOT power, because I can take your money and spend it how I want — AND, I can ignore you, make you feel unseen and unheard. I can take away your power.

*

but while living through it — while spluttering disbelief and rage and confusion in the days and weeks it played out, like a bad theatre show — I could see how this experience was, simultaneously, a multi-faceted glacier of truth; a clever onion with layers and layers that I could keep unpeeling. peel, chop, cry.

I could see that it was a gift — a masterclass from the universe meant to strip me naked, and leave me stranded — only so that I could rise again out of the fall of the tower and claim what was always mine; always untouchable: the clarity of my vision, and the force of my creative materializing power.

I’m here now — by recording this saga in tedious detail — to integrate these lessons: about the absolute necessity of cherishing my most precious resources in this life: that is, creative energy, attention, and commitment - and why I must never, ever override my instinct and intuition — even in the name of big dreams, or hopeful ambition, or love.

 

back to top

origins of a dream: a coffee shop love story

in order to explain why we stayed entangled in a bad situation for far too long, first, I have to tell you the dream.

in late 2021, my partner K and I met at a coffee shop in a historic part of Istanbul — he was the main barista there, and I was a traveler passing by — staying, for one month, in a fourth floor airbnb apartment right above his cafe. I was nearing the end of my two years of nomadic living, and in very depressed period of my life — but, I dragged myself downstairs everyday to do the bare minimum: have a cup of coffee, journal or draw, and chat with barista in simple english. I drew my first impressions of Istanbul while at that coffee shop.

K made me feel at ease and safe in ways that I couldn’t quite articulate back then (my intuition drew him as a dark bird). a few months later, I decided to end my two years of nomadic living, and move to Istanbul.

then, within half a year, I found myself (not without panic) in the most easeful and stable relationship of my life with K. even just a few months in, I drew it as the feeling of being safe. that following summer, we adopted our dog Luna — who I met, one monday morning, at that exact same cafe.

all this to say, cafes have played a significant role in my life, and our lives together. not only was it the space that literally connected us — as a two-human-one-dog family unit — but for me, throughout all of my travels through different cities and countries, cafes were one of the only spaces where I could be in the public world, and still be in solitude; deeply connected to my inner world and creative practice (not unlike… a website?!)

for K, coffee shops were a tangible materialization of his intense work ethic, his obsession with order, and his operationally-minded drive. over the last years, he had worked as a barista, a coffee shop manager/consultant, and opened several coffee shops for his then-boss. it was his dream to open his own cafe, and after years of being together, it became my dream, too.

then, in the last year or two, we had slowly started working together in doing digital work, too, as a designer/developer team, creating custom-built websites for complex client projects — laying the foundations for what would become otherworldly, which I write about here. the more we built digital spaces together — in which I led the vision, and he led the execution — the more I could feel our desire to create a physical space together, too.

(for context: K is an extremely grounding, future-oriented, manifesting generator, Capricorn stellium. his favorite thing to do with me is to talk about our future. he is the first man in my life who has done so, without triggering me to eventually abort that potential future).

in our future coffee shop, we said, he would manage the bar and cashier, oversee the daily business operations, hire and train the future baristas — and I would bake cakes and cookies, handletter the daily menu, create the branding, the aesthetics, the signage — and fill the space with art, sprawling plants, and the little magical, poetic details that would make our cafe unforgettable.

*

sidenote: years before I met K, in 2020, when I was living in Paris for a few months, I frequented a minimalist, tiny coffee shop tucked away in a corner — run by a couple — a French man and a Korean woman. he would chat with all the guests like it was his living room, and she would look after the tables, or come in and out with fresh cut flowers for the tables. even before I knew what I wanted, or believed it was possible to find a relationship in which I’d be happy, I could feel that I wanted that — to be creating beautiful physical vessel with someone I love, and to share it with others.

back to top

making the dream happen

the dream happened — only nothing at all like what we’d imagined.

so, not the dream, but a shadow version of the dream; an anti-dream.

a dream that makes you cry. so, a nightmare.

speaking the intention outloud

sometime in late August, I sat down in meditation and felt the shape of a desire form in my body. in the previous months, while doing digital work together, K was wishing outloud that he had his own coffee shop — something material and physical to do with his body. so I stated the intention outloud, in two or three separate sittings, over a week. all I said was: “I want K to open his own coffee shop.”

had I been even a little bit wiser, a little more careful in my practice of energetics, I would’ve known better than to speak an intention so open-ended and vague into the universe. but, I said it — just because that statement felt true. I mostly didn’t believe we had the conditions to make it actually happen. so I said, without much thought.

then it happened.

a business venture arrives

a week or two later, the seed of this idea arrived in the form of K’s two close friends, who K had known for over a decade. I’ll call them Cousin and Best Friend, because that’s who they were, to K.

K thought of Best Friend like a blood brother. Cousin is Best Friend’s biological cousin — hence why K also called this guy “Cousin.” (turkish man dynamics, or whatever.)

Best Friend is a chef, actor, and restoration architect — who K met when he took acting classes at age 18. K and Best Friend lived together as roommates, worked at other cafes together as barista and chef. over the last three years of my relationship with K, I’ve invited Best Friend and Cousin to dinner parties at our house, I’ve attended Best Friend’s theatre shows, and we’ve gone on barbecue excursions together in the forest, with Luna.

Cousin called K one night — saying that he was looking at commercial leasing spaces. Cousin had just left his job at an autopark and was looking to open a business — a shop or a cafe of some sort — and wanted K to join him. K and Best Friend had already been talking about opening a cafe together for many years.

the three of them decided that NOW was the time to start something.

I remember clearly the night those conversations began. after a long conversation, K and I figured out that he’d really rather open a cafe alone, or with me, but he felt loyal and obligated to his friends, and he wanted to support them. he had more experience than either of them when it came to cafes and coffee shop management — and so, he saw himself as someone to lead and guide them in this process.

their plan, at first, did not involve me in any way. that was fine with me. I remember walking around those weeks, levitating with a ballooning, honey-filled joy in my heart. I felt so excited for them — a pure sense of joy — that K could finally pursue one of his lifelong dreams with two old, close friends.

gathering the resources

but. the problem was that no one knew how much the whole thing would cost — and no one really had a significant amount of cash to invest. the Cousin sold a car, and pulled together around $8k. K and Best Friend were planning to take out bank loans to cover the rest of the starting capital. for a few weeks in August, they were circling around a commercial rental space — a corner shop just 5 minutes walking from our apartment, in our neighborhood. K had convinced them to choose a location close to our home — in a very central, busy part of Istanbul — with the idea he would be the main person working behind the bar, and opening the shop every morning.

then, their bank loans didn’t go through.

the landlord was waiting for a response.

so I told K that I could help — I could also invest around $8k. I just wanted to support my partner in this venture, even if it didn’t involve me.

after my own long, arduous journey of struggling to feel financially empowered in my chosen career path as an artist, I felt like I finally had a little bit of room to do something big with my resources — like "support my partner in opening a coffee shop.” it was a personal milestone for me to have that money, AND to not feel the need to hoard it out of fear of scarcity — and I wanted to give it to him. I didn’t expect it, or need it back.

so, with a budget of around $16k, the three of them would attempt to sign a lease, pay for a few month’s rent, do the renovations, buy all the cafe equipment and furniture, and set up the coffee shop for opening. it was a shoestring budget for a cafe — but we all believed that with a bit of resourcefulness, thriftiness, and creativity, we could do it. together, we could make it work.


our financial agreement

before I entered the picture, the three men had agreed to a 40/30/30 profit share of the cafe. their roles were agreed upon between them — K would be the cafe manager, head barista, and would working full shifts at the cafe (40%), Best Friend would be the dessert chef (30%), and Cousin would do the overflow — waiting the tables and handling the cash register (30%).

when I had talked about my investment, K asked me — what are your conditions? did I want to think of this investment as a “loan,” which I would get back — or did I want a stake in the business?

I said that I didn’t need the money back; I preferred a stake in the business. and, given that I was providing half of the total investment of 16k, I asked for an even share — 25% of the business. we had already discussed that I would be in charge of the branding, aesthetics, design, and decor — (that is, my professional work which made me the money in the first place).

K told Best Friend and Cousin that it wasn’t a 100% assumed certainty that I’d invest this money. what, really? they asked. they seem surprised. in hindsight, this assumption of my automatic buy-in (as the woman backing up her man, doing anything for him) makes me viscerally repulsed.

here’s where the problems began.

Best Friend was not excited about the 25% split proposal. he complaining that with a 25% even split each (instead of their previous 30%, so a 5% difference…), there would be no profits left to share between the four of us. he said that instead, they could give me 10% of the business — and then also return my investment money back, as a loan. it would be a split of 30 / 30 / 30 between the three of them, and 10% for me. (in other words: K shared his extra 10% with me).

okay, sure, I said. the profit share really didn’t matter to me, but I was dismayed at what this signaled — how much they valued and respected my energy and investment. but I reminded myself: all I wanted was just for this cafe to happen for K, and I wanted to contribute my energy to its creative, aesthetic process — and make it a beautiful place we could all be proud of.

I asked for a contract between the four of us, and I would prepare to send them the money. K started putting together a contract, and asked Cousin and Best Friend to sign it. they hemmed and hawed — ah, is a contract really necessary between old friends? — etc etc. we’ll do it later, they said.

in the meantime, they had decided on the space.

it was a corner shop with two walls of floor to ceiling windows, within 5 minutes walking of our apartment. it was previously a chicken shop, and so it needed a lot of renovation work. to keep it simple for tax purposes, the three men decided that the cafe would be a sole proprietorship in Best Friend’s name.

Best Friend signed a contract with the landlord for a 10 year lease.

back to top

all the red flags we ignored

the hallucinatory power of a shared dream is that if you’re not careful, it makes you blind to all the red flags — then, to the subtle and significant ways in which a shared dream diverges into irreconcilable differences.

we all wanted to open a cafe, but the cafe represented vastly different things to each of us. sure, everyone wanted the cafe to be successful and make money. for me, it was a materialization of my creative, artistic energy into a physical space. for K, it was a vessel for his work ethic, his vision, and standards of professionalism and integrity — a chance to pour himself, completely, into a physical business he owned.

for Cousin and Best Friend, we later realized, it was something else entirely. it was an expensive playground for their fragile egos. it was a grandiose, desperate, last-ditch attempt to get rich fast, while lacking the confidence or vision to build something lasting. it was a theatrical performance of owning a cafe — a show given to the small audience of their friends — while they played the role of big bad bosses.

giving voice to my hesitation

because we had a small budget of 16k, everything happened in a rush. this was part of the problem. K asked me when I was going to send the money — they had just signed the contract, and Cousin needed cash to pay the deposit and to get the renovation work started, so that the cafe could open as soon as possible — and begin making money.

I remember that day clearly. it was all about to happen, I was having doubts.

I said to K, I really want you to open a cafe, you know I support you 100%. I love your friends as people but… I don’t know… I don’t trust them.

you don’t trust them… he said, so… you don’t want to support this cafe? we just signed the contract, so we wouldn’t be able to move forward…

in the aftermath of this event, we’ve returned to that conversation many times, and each time we talk about it, he apologizes again — for pressuring me while I was having doubts. I was excited, he said, and caught in the momentum and energy of the moment. he was trying to “make it happen.” his friends had verbally made agreements to us — “return Kening’s 8k, give her 10% of the profits” — but there was nothing signed and formalized on paper. we only had their word.

in retrospect, reflecting on this situation from the lens of human design — an energetics system that has unlocked a lot for me, over the years — I see that my self-projected authority (finding my truth through what I say) had spoken outloud what my intuition knew about these people. but, we were both blinded by excitement, momentum, and possibility.

so, I ignored my own voice. I sent them the money.


arguing while buying cafe furniture & equipment

in the next few weeks, the three men ran around the city buying and haggling for what they needed to open the cafe on our small budget.

we quickly discovered that our aesthetic vision for the cafe drastically differed — Cousin and Best Friend preferred the cheapest, flashiest things possible, which seemed to us, gaudy and showy — while K and I preferred subtle, natural, and understated.

in front of his two friends, K was my spokesperson. K texted me photos of different options and reminded them that I had the final say. they argued about everything, but, every night, K still came home, at night, with excitement.

one day, when we open our own cafe, it’ll be me and you going around looking at equipment and choosing wall paneling and furniture, he said.

we’ll argue about everything, and then we’ll make up, and it’ll be so much fun…


the non-existent budget

as they started spending money, I told K that we needed to make a budget spreadsheet, and keep track of all receipts and expenses, so that we knew where the money was going. K asked them to do clear accounting, and send receipts.

yeah yeah, Cousin said, I’m keeping track of everything, I’ll send it over later.

over the next weeks, we asked again. several times.

of course, he never did. until the very end.

the floor plan they ignored

one night, K and I spent hours one night drawing up a floor plan for the cafe — calculating in exact centimeters where all the equipment and tables and chairs would go. here’s what I drew.

a vision of our cafe, as we pictured it in our minds. the final result looked nothing like this.

the massive pastry case

then. Best Friend insisted on buying a massive pastry glass case — more than double the size that we had alloted to it in our bar plan — because it was the cheapest, he said. but really, I know, he just wanted a large container to put his ego.

WTF, are we opening a coffee shop, or a bakery? I asked K. why is he ignoring the floor plan?

eventually, we compromised on a (slightly) smaller pastry case — but which was still much larger than our original plans. I redrew the bar according to show what it would look like.

the original (our plan)

the massive pastry case

the espresso machine they couldn’t afford

in the meantime, K found a used, high-quality espresso machine at half retail price. they went in and looked at it. Best Friend and Cousin hesitated to commit to paying for this machine — saying that it seemed too expensive.

apparently, they had forgotten that we were opening a cafe — not a sandwich shop.

by the following week, the seller had sold it to someone else.

the logo they dismissed

one of the only things we agreed on — was that they liked a name for the cafe I had come up with: mantis.

I thought of it one day while talking to K about how the female mantis, after copulation, bites off the head of the male mantis and eats him.

I worked on a mockups of the brand color palette and logo design. I didn’t like the idea of including a literal “mantis” in the graphics — it felt too on-the-nose — but they wanted a real mantis logo, so I drew my minimalist versions. I choose a typography that felt cozy and sharp at the same time, and took inspiration from the orchid mantis and the powers of camouflage.

certainly, what I drew was not a finished design, nor was it my best design. it was a work in progress.

K was the one in daily communication with his friends — so I asked him to send these 3 rough draft versions to share with them.

their responses:

BEST FRIEND: “are there any other options?”
[silence]
K: “Cousin, what do you think?”
COUSIN: “it’s really bad, yahh… let’s just use the text and be done with it.”

I remember noticing that I felt the sort of vulnerability I hadn’t felt in a long time — the feeling of being judged by people who couldn’t even see and recognize that you exist.

they were not obligated to like my logo, nor my design aesthetics. this wasn’t the problem. the problem was that in my many years of doing design work for clients, I’ve never had anyone respond to my work in such a dismissive manner.

if I even sensed that it was a possibility to receive this kind of feedback, then I would’ve never worked with a client — no matter how much money they were willing to pay me.

okay, but these men were not clients.

this was not a client project. I was not working for them. just because I paid for half the venture did not mean that they were obligated to like my designs. but they did need to respect my work and creative expertise. getting this one sentence dismissal felt like being slapped in the face.

K first says he wants out

it was after this text exchange about the logo — that K said he wanted out. he wanted to exit the cafe venture, end the friendship with both of them, and get my money back.

if it’s one thing I cannot tolerate, it’s disrespect, he said.

they’re allowed to disrespect me — I can laugh it off. but they can’t disrespect you. the first time is the last time.

I told him he was being too extreme, too harsh. just because they were insensitive, blundering cave men with no aesthetic sensibilities didn’t mean that we needed to call the whole thing off. I felt too invested in the dream; I didn’t want him to lose the venture and two decades-long friendships — just on principle, just in defense of me, or just to uphold his gangster sense of honor.

for him, this moment was a big violation of a boundary — and a signal of what was to come. perhaps it’s because he loved me that he could see it so clearly — whereas, those past weeks, he was able to brush off the series of micro-violations against him — the hijacking of our floor plan and bar plan, their hesitation to buy a espresso machine.

within a day, his attitude towards his friends and the entire venture became cold and distant — like his inner fire literally froze into a block of ice. he lost most of his enthusiasm, and was withdrawing from the group. in these weeks, the cafe had ongoing renovation work — there was construction, electric work, plumbing work, etc, constantly. K came and went to the cafe to oversee the contractors. then he came home.

I spent a few days trying to thaw and soften him.

I wanted him to have his dream; our dream.

I brushed off the “small” violations against me. this was my mistake.

if we’re going to do this, we need to give it our best shot, I said. we can’t half-ass this.

okay, okay, he said.

the calm before the storm

a week or so later, we left for a 10 day roadtrip through the south of turkey — a trip we had planned for months, which I captured in a visual diary. within a few days, the sour taste of this cafe friction disappeared into the background.

before we left, K sent them a contract to sign, again. it restated, in writing, our previous financial and profit share agreements. they had delayed signing it for weeks — blaming the whirlwind of events — but K was pressuring them again.

we’ll look at it and sign it when you come back, Best Friend says.

in those weeks, they were spending money left and right, but had not yet bought an espresso machine — a clear symbol of how much they valued K’s coffee expertise and standards, and the initial agreement that they were opening “a cafe.”

what’s my purpose there if there’s no espresso machine? K said. I don’t need to be there to press a button on a filter machine….

I sent them edited logo files — of just the wordmark and color palette — to create the signage so that it could be ready for the opening, when we came back.

during our vacation, Cousin and Best Friend barely called K to ask for his opinion on anything — except, maybe, once or twice. they reported that they didn’t want to “disturb our vacation.”

but in reality, they saw our vision and aesthetic preferences as static interference.

while we were gone, they were free to do whatever they wanted.

back to top

the storm: betrayal and speechless rage

nothing really prepared me for what was going to happen next, though, in retrospect, it seems inevitable.

pushing me out of the partnership

when we returned from our trip, Best Friend asked to meet with K. Best Friend decided that they didn’t want me to be a stakeholder in the business — they wanted to strip me of my 10% profit share, and divide the cafe business evenly between the three of them: 30/30/30. I don’t know why he didn’t say it to my face.

in other words, for an extra 3% each — they wanted to get rid of my role in the partnership. yes, they were going to return the 8k as a loan, they said.

K wanted to quit, then and there, on the spot, he said. but, because of how I had asked him to temper his extreme reactions, instead, he stayed silent. he came home and asked me what I wanted to do.

I felt the kind of rage that burned so hot it made me cry — a rage that comes from feeling completely diminished and disregarded as less than a full being. along with that rage, I felt betrayal, confusion, disbelief, shock, and helplessness.

it was clear to me that this wasn’t about the money, or the 3% profit share. their intention was to strip me of all voice, power, and authority — in a venture that my investment money helped make possible. they took my monetary resources, carelessly spent it like man-children buying toys for their new playpen, and then decided that I was worthless after my money had been spent; I was just a hovering, nitpicking woman meddling in their manly business. they decided that it was time to erase me from any and all decision-making power in the venture. this was what ejecting me from the partnership meant — it was an act of silencing my voice.

there was also an underlying tone of misogyny, here, that I couldn’t shake off. it was as if they couldn’t fathom the idea that a woman helped make this venture financially possible. the subtext I got was that it was okay to dishonor an agreement made with a woman — and there was very little I could do to fight back.

K held me while I anger-cried — almost every day that week — and asked me what I wanted to do.

I oscillated between wanting to quit the whole thing — and feeling trapped by the sunk cost — all the energy, time, and money we spent already on this venture.


discovering the balcony we never wanted

then, we discovered that they had been very busy while we were away. not only did they buy the massive pastry case, they continued minimizing the dimensions of the cafe bar — in order to make room for a balcony. they weren’t just pushing me out; they were physically making less space for K.

from the beginning, K and I were against having a balcony — it was October, and winter was approaching — and a balcony meant that we’d only have two small tables of indoor seating, like an afterthought. a balcony was not in our vision of a cozy cafe as refuge from the chaos of the city — it was their way of catering to smokers in the dead of winter.

while we were gone, without a word to us, they spent the investment money on building a balcony — and with it, they constructed a sliding glass panel door — which wafted in a breeze of cold air anytime it was opened and closed.

then, with the last remaining drops of money, they bought K a cheap espresso machine and coffee grinder machine — a surprise for K, they said.

back to top

a midnight confrontation with 3 turkish men

within a week, it was eating me alive. I went to bed fuming every night, and finally, I couldn’t hold it in anymore. I asked for a conversation with them.

the four of us met at a nearby bakery at 10pm on a weekday night, and I remember how my heart was pounding, while I wondered if I had enough words in my Turkish vocabulary to express what I wanted to say to these men.

they arrived, totally oblivious, sat down and lit a cigarette… while I exploded in a cold rage.

I demanded to know why they took my money, and dishonored our agreement of partnership. after I had trusted and supported them as K’s closest friends, all these years, after doing my best to support this venture, why did they treat me with such disrespect and deceit? was it because I was a foreigner? a woman?

Cousin, stunned by my outburst, got up after 10 minutes and left — apparently, he felt overwhelmed by my emotional outburst.


Best Friend’s defense

Best Friend, meanwhile, spent the next hours putting up a defense — he displayed indignance that at the idea that he had a prejudice against working with women, and recounted evidence of the contrary. he made a long argument that he saw me as “a part” of K — we were one entity — and that, if anything, we, as a couple, should’ve made a contract with each other.

by his account, I had no soveriegnty as my own human being, with control and agency over my own money — I was an Eve made from the rib of Adam, and counted as a “part” of him.

Best Friend said that he had always wanted to share the business only with his two closest friends — K and Cousin — but that he felt silenced when I showed up with the investment money they needed, and conditions of my own. so yes, he agreed to my conditions of 10%, even though he didn’t really want to extend partnership to me.

then, weeks later, after all this work was done and we were approaching the opening day of the cafe — he couldn’t shake the discomfort that this venture didn’t feel right as a four-way partnership. it upset his stomach, he said. so now, he had to say something.

in other words — now that he had a business registered in his name, a brick and mortar shop built with other people’s money, and a massive pastry case to flaunt his ego, he felt like he could open his mouth and say, “well, yeah… I changed my mind…”

allowing myself to be pacified

the problem with all this is… in spite of everything, I wanted to forgive Best Friend, just as much as I wanted this cafe dream to work. K treated Best Friend like a brother. Best Friend stayed in our apartment, watering our plants while we were away. Best Friend helped me out when K was away at military service for six months. Best Friend was supposed to be best man at our wedding.

maybe that was the problem. the stakes felt so high. the cost of admitting the situation fully — acknowledging the level of disrespect and betrayal that we felt — would mean irreparable damage to our relationship. it would mean that all that energy and investment and years amounted to… nothing?

so, over the next few hours, until 1 am in the morning, I let Best Friend listen to my rage, and I let him talk me out of my state. I let him apologize for his unprofessionalism, I let him defend his integrity and re-affirm that he cherished and valued our relationship, and his relationship with K, and that he didn’t want this cafe business to interfere with our friendship.

I allowed myself to entertain the idea that it wasn’t a malicious betrayal, but an act of total thoughtlessness, and lack of foresight. I let him charm me, because I wanted peace. K, on the other hand, was mostly quiet, and skeptical.


Cousin’s outburst

a few days later, at 10pm at night, in the second floor of a bakery filled with their cigarette smoke, we met with Cousin again and repeated a similar confrontation — except this time, it was like dealing with a hot tempered child in the body of a 35 year old man. he said that after our conversation a few nights ago, he cried like a baby on the car ride home, while calling his contacts. and by the way, I found your money, he said, as if it was that easy for him. as in — he found an aquaintance who was willing to lend him 8k.

that night, Cousin kept saying things to diminish the value of my investment — his friend gave him another few grand, and that guy wasn’t making demands about partnership, plus there was the 8k he put in after selling his car — so really, my money only amounted to something like 25% of the total capital — and, how dare I get on my high horse about it — clearly, I’m replacable, and he could’ve found that money anywhere…

Cousin said that he felt backstabbed by the fact that K and I, who he thought of as his “brother and sister” — could make such a big deal over a tiny amount as a 10% profit share. this was a deep damage to his trust, he said, and he wasn’t sure that he could continue this business with us.

K and I sat in shock, and Best Friend sat in stoic silence. like some wise sage, he took some of the blame for instigating this conflict with his indecisiveness around agreeing to give me 10%, then changing his mind.

it was an absolutely ridiculous conversation — and I knew that, even then. the fact that this grown man was turning the tables and victimizing himself, using his temper tantrum as a weapon against us — it made me angry.

the compulsion to be a peacemaker

but, in the last days, I had already decided — despite K’s skepticism — that we weren’t backing out. I wanted to see it through to the end. now that everyone was arguing and fighting and angry at everyone, and I felt the compulsve urge to ignore my own boundaries and needs, and to be the peacemaker — to do some emotional labor, and massage some communication skills to these three combative men — to smooth things over, the way I was conditioned to, as a woman. (clearly, a deeply engrained, terribly damaging habit learned from childhood).

I tried to convince everyone to return to the vision. to make a decision about whether or not they were in — or out. I said that K and I were committed to supporting this venture, together, as best as we could, and then I asked for my money back — as a 12 month loan over 2025, with a small amount ($500) of interest. for the nth time, I said I wanted it in writing (…this never happened).

when I brought up the subject of the logo, Best Friend and Cousin said that they dropped the subject, because they ran out of money and time to think about signage. they weren’t dismissing the subject, or me, but preoccupied by the renovation work. we’d return to this later, together.

so, some way or the other, that night ended with us standing around the cafe — the three Turkish men taking turns giving each other manly pat-hugs — then standing around on the sidewalk, chit chatting about mugs, plates, and tea saucers.

*

in retrospect, this explosion and reconciliation cycle reminded me of the aborted endings of toxic relationships — in which you get back together again, thinking that things could be different, that it could still work out, somehow, if only we tried our best. I was unwilling to accept total loss, or total death — of the cafe dream, of the friendships — so I clung onto a small amount of hope. K, being far more decisive and less forgiving — was doubtful and reluctant, even then. but he agreed to stick it out, for me, for us.

the truth was that by then, it was already too late. we were way past the point of no return. as bleak as it sounds to admit, there was actually nothing there to salvage, because the very foundations upon which to build a business — shared values, vision, and professional and personal integrity — was all wrong.

the cafe had not even opened, and we had already lost.

the cafe opens, but I feel only grief


less than a week later, on October 23rd, 2024, the cafe opened.

I’ll remember this day always, because it’s my brother’s birthday, and the first day of Scorpio season. my birthday is towards the end of Scorpio season, on November 19th. if I were to describe the cafe betrayal and subsequent fall out as the experience of falling from the tower, then that entire fall happened within the container of Scorpio season.

by the time my birthday arrived, everything would be over. I would be in the US with my parents, experiencing minor daily hives breakouts, and emotionally preparing myself for an unexpected surgery to remove a growing benign mass in my body. by then, the cafe situation would’ve been temporarily forgotten — in my body, but briefly out of my mind.

the day the cafe opened, I sat with a notebook and my computer, and drank my first cup of coffee. I tried to work, but I couldn’t focus. I felt nervous anytime a passerby walked down the street and glanced inside. then, I felt a spike of panic when our first customers arrived. although this cafe looked absolutely nothing like I had imagined, and none of my creative energy or visions — it still was created, in part, from my resources. I couldn’t help but still feel invested.

then, all of a sudden, K was gone from the home 16 hours a day. he left at 7am to open the cafe, and closed it at 11pm, and came home. those first few days, I left our dog Luna at the cafe, in hopes that her smiling face through the glass windows would draw the attention of passerbys.

then I went home. I sat and worked alone in a dark, empty apartment.

I felt like I should be happy at the apparent fruition of a long time shared dream — I stated outloud that I wanted “K to open his own cafe,” and then it happened. nothing more, nothing less.

instead, I found that I couldn’t stop crying. the waves of rage, shock, and betrayal had subsided into attempts at peace — and now, after it all, I felt only grief. the emotional truth was that I felt so totally devalued, like I had already lost so much creative energy, trust, time, and money — and now — even for a day, or two, or three — I lost the presence of my partner and dog.

monstera as metaphor of creative energy

the cafe opened on a wednesday. they planned an opening party for that sunday.

in those days leading up to our opening party, I was trying to decide whether or not to give the cafe a gift I had promised, weeks earlier — one of the two monstera plants that flourished in our apartment.

but, I found that when I looked at my monstera plants, cultivated over three years of living in Istanbul, I couldn’t bear the thought of giving it away. it felt viscerally, bodily wrong — like giving away a child to an irresponsible stranger.

my body, again, was telling me what my mind couldn’t face.

my monstera represented a figment of my creative energy — tenderly cultivated over time, in living, tangible form. it thrived in the safety of our home. I couldn’t put it in an environment where its very existence and being felt threatened, devalued, exploited, and unsafe. a part of my childish, hopeful mind thought that giving my plants or my art to the cafe would help me make it feel more “mine.”

my body told me that the atmosphere and air of the place was toxic.

so, instead, I went to a plant shop and bought a monstera. I left that one at the cafe.


the opening party

that sunday, we threw an opening party. Best Friend, K, and Cousin all invited their friends to come. I drew the animated invitations — only because K asked me to (as a personal favor for me, he said), and invited a handful of people.

   

that sunday, I stayed at the cafe for a few hours, while K stood working behind the bar, and Best Friend sat on the balcony smoking with his theatre friends, who came in and out, smoking and laughing. Best Friend had made sandwiches, and a dozen different desserts, cookies, and cakes to fill the massive pastry case — most of which would still be there, days later, growing stale.

one of K’s friends commented that it was as if K was the silent worker, while Best Friend and Cousin laughed and smoked and shook hands, like big bosses. for me, the party carried with it that terrible dissonance of feeling deeply unhappy on a surface-level, happy occasion.

that night, I woke up at 3am with my first full body outbreak of hives — angry red welts covering my entire body, all the way to my face, like being chased by a swarm of wasps. three days later, I had an even worse episode.

again — my body knew. my body was staging a massive protest at the boundaries of my skin, rejecting the way it had been energetically violated, and telling me to please, for god’s sake, do something about it.

then came the bitter end

the ending unfolded in less than two weeks, from Oct 27-Nov 6th. I feel exasperated and exhausted even now, writing this, months later.

looking back, I see how we were incapable of leaving any sooner, because we would’ve always wondered... did we give it our best shot? could we have made it work? could it have been any different? one thing that K and I both have in common is the stamina and will to “fight to the death” — in love, or work, or for an ideal we believed in. it was important for both of us to be decisively committed to something — committed with 100% of our being — not 80 or 90%, and certainly not halfway.

after the opening party, K continued to arrive at the cafe in the early mornings, working behind the bar until the evenings. Cousin arrived in the afternoons, while Best Friend wandered in and out as he pleased. I went to the cafe everyday, for a few hours, to spend time with K — because otherwise, he was never home.

in spite of the reconciliatory conversations of those prior weeks, I was still rage-crying everyday. the brief excitement of the opening party had passed, and K was unhappy. he looked around the cafe — at the bar, the equipment, the decor, and said — there’s nothing of me or you here. what did we decide? the color of ceiling paint. the chairs. the shade of wood paneling. that’s it. nothing else is anything remotely like what we wanted.

I’ll stay here just for 6 months or a year, until we make back your investment money. then I’ll leave, he said.

so, in other words, I said, you’re going to do prisoner labor for the money I gave them under false premises, which they still owe me?

yes, but this is my fault, and my responsibility. I can choose to do this… he said.

the death blow was a $10 logo

by then, the cafe had been open for over a week, and we still didn’t have signage. K used a template on Canva and printed out a menu. Best Friend brought a chalkboard sign, and scribbled some words on it. I felt zero desire to help.

then, one evening, Cousin turned to us and said — I have good news, we found some signage that we can buy for cheap from a cafe that’s closing. we’ll have our own signage up soon.

oh, I said, tentatively... so … do you have a logo for it?

yeah, we picked one we liked, he said. no word about the notion that a logo could possibly have anything remotely to do with me.

Cousin got out his phone, and showed K and I an image.

what I saw was — I do not exaggerate — the ugliest logo I have ever seen in my life. it was MANTIS COFFEE SHOP, written in three different fonts — a hodgepodge, frankensteined thing which resembled a musty, 90s-era basement gym infested with roaches. it looked like a failed sports brand — not even a failed coffee shop.

I was silent.

I looked at K. he looked back at me like a zombie. he shook his head as if to say — don’t bother.

we both stood there as if slapped in the face, dumbstruck for words. apparently, they had showed K this logo weeks prior — it was a $10 thing they commissioned from a guy on Instagram. K had firmly rejected it. now Cousin and Best Friend had decided — unanimously, between the two of them — that this was to be the new identity of our coffee shop. all of their friends thought it was cool, so, based on this crowd-sourced opinion, it must be great.

those prior weeks, I had felt, so much, the relentless assault of rage, betrayal, and grief — that now, a new emotion came. now, I felt a visceral repulsion and disgust.

the problem wasn’t the logo. this logo was the culmination and manifestation of the true identity of the business venture we had entangled ourselves in — one in which we had zero voice in. the logo painted a true picture of a cafe that was barely even a cafe — it was the cheaply constructed, sports car playtoy of two overgrown man-children.

in that moment, the enchantment finally broke.

I knew — in my body — that I would never let myself be in the same room as that logo. ever. again.

I even felt a flood of shame — that everything I had given of myself and my resources, the money which, symbolically, represented the fruits of what I forged from a decade of standing in my creative integrity, fighting for what I believed in — had been so deceived and hijacked to support the birth of such a thoughtless, meaningless entity that had absolutely nothing to do with me, my partner K, or the values we stood for.

I say this with the clarity of hindsight now.

but back then… back then, I was mostly dumbstruck and disgusted.

the last stand

a few days later, K and I decided to quit. he was leaving the three way partnership.

and, in truth, it was never really a partnership to begin with — they used my money, ignored our voices, and, despite countless requests, never signed any of our contracts. and so, we had no paper trails — and no leverage. but by then, none of this really mattered to us. K and I just wanted out. we wanted to wash our hands clean, and leave this ugly mess behind us.

K, being the Capricorn stellium he is, planned to stay a few more weeks to help them with the bar — and to train Cousin to take over as a barista. in his mind, it was his “last favor” for old friends — before he was planning to end the friendship.

leading up to that confrontation, K and I made a list of all the things in the coffee shop that had completely strayed from what we had initially agreed upon —


floor plan
bar plan
bar equipment
pastry case
budget (?!?)
financial split
management
contract (!?!)
balcony
glass walls
concept
decor
logo & design
espresso machine

in other words, everything. nothing in the cafe was anything like what we had agreed or discussed in the initial weeks of the venture.

in those last few days, K had two conversations with his friends.

  1. in the first conversation, he told them he was exiting.

  2. in the second conversation, he asked for my investment money back.


I’m reporting this secondhand, but in the first conversation — when K told them of our/his decision, they mostly just nodded and expressed regret that K was leaving. they assumed that the financial agreement — a 12 month repayment — was to stay the same.

a day or two later, after talking to my brother, I jerked awake — as if waking up out of bad dream — and realized that I had every right to demand my money back, now, not spread out over 12 months. afterall, didn’t Cousin brag that he could find my money anywhere — that my investment was negligible and replaceable?

that week, Cousin had finally organized all the expenses, and bashfully admitted that my investment was 50% of the total capital — not 25%, as he had once claimed. I had no intention of seeing either of them ever again. so K sat them down for this second conversation. he asked for my 8k back.

I had zero expectations that they would give it back.

I wasn’t there to see it, but apparently, once money was the contested thing, the conversation devolved quickly.

they refused — saying that they couldn’t give back the money now. Best Friend argued that we had already “resolved” this disagreement in our previous midnight conversations with me — all of this was bridge under the water. Cousin said, “but I offered your money back that night, you could’ve accepted it then.”

K — being the Knight of Swords that he is — didn’t give up the fight, or seek a diplomatic resolution. and I didn’t expect him to. we had already lost all that we were going to lose, and K refused to lose his sense of honor.

they exchanged harsh words. then curses. Best Friend told him to get the fuck out of the cafe — this cafe isn’t yours. K threw the keys across the table, informed his best friends that they were liars, scammers, and thieves… and left.

*

so, that’s how it ended.

not with a whimper, but with a bang.

we never heard a word from them again, nor a saw a cent of my money back.

every now and then, while walking with Luna, we’ll stroll past the main street of our neighborhood, turn our heads to look at that cafe, tucked away in the corner of a side street, marked by a round white sign with that abominable logo. and mostly, I feel relief.

on betrayal and self-betrayal


even though, throughout my twenties, I’ve experienced variations of having my voice ignored and my boundaries violated in toxic romantic relationships, this cafe experience was the first time it had happened, so viscerally and blatantly, in context of my creative work and professional life. it was no mistake that it had to happen like this, by men who I believed I could trust, in a foreign country, culture, and language. I needed to know, in my body, what it felt like to be voiceless.

and while I describe this situation as betrayal — because that’s what it felt like — to betray, they needed to see me as someone worth betraying. and they didn’t.

months after the fact, what kept me in a loop of judgement and pain was revisiting all the ways in which I had betrayed myself. I felt ashamed by the small and big ways I had overrided my instincts, my intuition, my voice, my needs, my emotions — in the name of a shiny dream that resembled what I deeply wanted, but was really was just a full body nightmare in disguise.

back to top

the sacredness of boundaries

still, I see this nightmare as a wake-up gift.

it has done so much to teach me about why boundaries matter — not as a last resort defense mechanism in toxic situations, but as moment-to-moment wayfinding, sensing guides that can help me discern where to even bring my presence, energy, or attention. boundaries create safe containers around my fluid, expansive, magical creative being. its structure creates the energetic shield that allows me to stay soft.

in the past, I’ve felt ashamed and pressured for not having “better boundaries.” but now, I understand that my commitment and loyalty, my abundance of creative resources, and my urge for generosity IS my greatest gift. boundaries are not about building rigid walls to keep the world at an arms length. boundaries are like fireflies — venturing around me, letting me know where it’s safe to land, to commit, and stay present for a while. boundaries help me keep my entire ecosystem in a state of nourishment and flow, so that I can keep giving from a place of abundance.

this is why I’m not on social media, why I’ve given everything to building my website as a digital world, to creating the business container that is otherworldly — and why I’m careful with who I choose to work with as private clients. I know that I work best when I’m all or nothing — and so, defining clear containers isn’t optional — it’s a pre-requisite to sustainable energy.

in the case of this cafe situation, I was pouring my life energy into a plastic toy bucket that had a big hole at the bottom.

on vision, clarity, and alignment

you could say that the obvious learning, here, is around clarity and alignment.

this is a study of how doing business with friends can easily go wrong — when trust is assumed and implicit — before agreements are made explicit. you assume that people keep their word as a matter of integrity and honor — until they don’t. we came with different visions, wanting to build radically different businesses, and we didn’t even know how at odds they were with one another.

it’s a study of compromise — how both K and I put aside our own violated boundaries for the sake of the other, in the name of friendship, or love, or for a shared dream. I gave them the money not because I trusted them, but because I trusted my partner K, and I wanted him to be successful. now I know: even an drop of my energy in the wrong place — is a drainage to myself, to him, and to us.

back to top

recognition is permission and power

but, ultimately, I think the greatest lesson and gift I learned from this experience has to do with the ideas of recognition and discernment.

if boundaries are the containers we draw around our relationship with other people and things outside of ourselves, in order to honor our sense of self, than recognition is the key that helps us define the shape of those boundaries. recognition grants permission and access, preceding and informing all boundaries.

  1. what is recognition? acknowledgement, appreciation. to put it simply — the feeling of being seen.

  2. what is discernment? clear sensitive judgement. or, the ability to see clearly.


it is the essential pre-requisite for any kind of personal, creative, energetic, or financial exchange. recognition is a word I’ve reflected on a lot, in the context of learning about the system of human design — and through working with my particular design as a self-projected projector, and my strategy of waiting for recognition, and invitation.

I’ve grappled with the surface-level passivity of this practice for many years, and eventually realized that being recognized helps me be efficient and directed with my creative energy. recognition and discernment helps me form the right boundaries to prevent me from depleting energy on the wrong people, projects, or endeavors.


recognition, money, and power

this cafe experience taught me — in a physical, visceral way — what it felt like to be so deeply un-recognized — unseen. unheard. unacknowledged.

recognition is NOT something that you can buy with investment money, or simply by being the life partner of their “best friend.” I had believed, at some level, that my 8k investment would grant me decision making power, and a voice. but instead, they took the money, and showed me how I had no power. their lack of recognition — lack of seeing me — combined with a lack of integrity and respect — was what made me feel so disempowered.

I realized that recognition is power, while money is a byproduct.

this applies both ways. let me explain.

when a student or client invites me to work with them, it’s because they see and recognize what I have to offer them — they both recognize my innate power, and empower me to serve them. it’s a two way channel.

if I turn down a client job — no matter the dollar amount, it’s because I don’t feel recognized or seen, or I don’t recognize them as the right client for me. I’m asserting my power and agency to say no.

my journey of integrating art, creativity and business was really about building the right containers to channel my wealth of resources INTO a clear exchange with others — where money is the byproduct. recognition and discernment is the pre-requisite. it makes this exchange feel honorable and full of integrity, for everyone.

another way to frame it — is that recognition and power is about the practice of visibility.

visibility is NOT about self-promotion, or insisting that you’re seen by others.

visibility is about seeing — then, being seen for the way you see.

the reversal of creative business flow

what I experienced in this cafe experience was a total reversal/inverse of what I spent a decade building and integrating: an aligned flow between my energetic, creative, and business resources.

the money/resources I invested in the cafe had flowed TO ME through working with aligned clients and students who recognized me for my voice, vision, and gifts.

the intention behind that money was to build a physical creative vessel (a cafe) where I could continue to share my artistic resources with others — by building a beautiful space, by helping to nurture its success, and magnetizing more resources to it (including loyal customers, attention, and money).

instead, I gave away my resources to men who completely disregarded them, who were incapable of seeing me, my voice, vision, or gifts.

I made money — through being visible.

I gave that money away — to feel totally invisible.

after notes: a death and intiation

actually, I do know what invisibility feels like. I grew up in an immigrant cultural programming that measured self-worth by how much money you made in your annual paycheck, how many elite degrees you’ve accumulated, or how much social status you’ve accrued through the things you can afford with that money. and while I know that underlying all of this is a desire for safety and security admist generations of inherited trauma, it’s also true that growing up, I was praised for my math test scores, but never for my art or writing — at least, not by the people whose recognition I wanted the most. I didn’t want them to praise me, or tell me I’m amazing — I only wanted them to see me.

my creativity felt worthless in the both the materialist sense of the world, and in a deeply engrained, child part of my brain — because it didn’t offer a simple, straightforward way to produce money, which, in some twisted logic, meant that I wasn’t deserving of love.

but then, wow, I did it. I spent most of my adult life rebelling against the idea that being an artist meant accepting a life of scarcity — I forcefully shattered the idea that creative energy was meaningless and powerless in a capitalist, material world. it took me so many years to fix the bugs in my head, to stop feeling deep shame around money, to stop hating hating money as an oppressive force — and understand that creativity is not the poor, ugly sister of money; creativity is the mother of money.

so, I’ve found it ironic and deeply funny that growing up, money seemed like the solution for invisibility. having money meant LOOK AT ME, I EXIST. but now that I had made enough of it to give it away — on my own terms, as an artist — the journey only brought me back to the old wound of feeling so invisible, devalued, and unseen for my gifts. this was the universe’s clever onion gift to me. I’m amazed at its poetry.

there is no solution for feeling unseen by others.

there is only one single choice — you choose to see yourself, or not.

I’ve made tremendous leaps in the last years — from bashfully hiding parts of myself, to fully owning my visibility, and claiming my voice. it was just after this cafe death that I birthed otherworldly, and started dreaming and imagining what our own cafe — which will happen one day — might look and feel like.

I’ve grown so much, such that what I experienced in those few weeks was a total regression and reversal — like having my head shoved underwater, and briefly drowning in my own childlike helplessness. the experience of being silenced, devalued, and robbed by men — and all of the rage, loss, and grief that it triggered in me — I now see that it as one of the greatest deaths and initations that I could’ve ever received.

it’s a detox through suffocation. it’s a cleansing fire. it’s a reminder — like getting tattooed on every surface of skin on my body — that nothing and no one can ever touch my creative soveriegnty, silence my voice, or diminish the sacredness of my creative vision. it’s my physical and psychic body staging a rebellion.

it tells me that it wants to be reborn a monster. it’s a full throat, primal being scream. and I can feel that I’m just getting started. this is just another beginning.
